title: Randomness you can trust
summary: Pseudo-random generators, modulo bias, and how to test an RNG.

cards.title: Computers can't flip coins
cards.body:
A **pseudo-random number generator** (PRNG) is a tiny machine with a hidden **state**. Each call scrambles the state and hands you a number. Same starting state (the **seed**), same sequence, every time.

That's useful for replays and testing. But a game's outcomes must be **unpredictable** and **fair**, so slot studios use certified RNGs, and regulated markets test them against published standards (GLI-11 is a well-known one).

cards.title: A modern PRNG in 10 lines
cards.body: PCG32: a 64-bit LCG for the state, then a scrambling step for the output. The app's tests check it against the official reference output.

cards.title: The bug in rng() % n
cards.body: This is the most common randomness bug in game code, and it's invisible unless you count.

cards.title: The fix
cards.body: `-n` on an unsigned number wraps around to 2³² − n, so `(-n) % n` is 2³² mod n: the size of the unfair leftover. Rejecting raw values below it leaves an exact multiple of n.

cards.title: Testing a generator
cards.body: The **chi-square** statistic measures how far the counts are from perfectly even. Then watch the final step: a test can pass while a real flaw hides elsewhere.

cards.question: A generator outputs 0..7 equally often. You compute `r % 3`. Which result is least likely?
cards.explain: 0 comes from {0, 3, 6}, 1 from {1, 4, 7}, but 2 only from {2, 5}: 2 chances out of 8 instead of 3.

cards.question: Why is the LCG's lowest bit 1, 0, 1, 0...?
choices: Odd multiplier and odd increment: each step flips the parity
cards.explain: With x = a·x + c (mod 2³²) and both a and c odd, the parity of x flips every step. The low bits of power-of-two LCGs have very short cycles. That's why modern generators scramble their output.
